content: Septic arthritis is an acute joint infection that leads to destructive damage to the articular space. It is the most prevalent non-degenerative joint disease in developing countries. Infants and preschool-aged children, particularly boys, are the most susceptible to this condition. Additionally, septic arthritis disproportionately affects individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. While systemic corticosteroids combined with antibiotic therapy may be beneficial in treating septic arthritis, even after the infection is eradicated with antibiotics, the inflammatory process can still result in residual joint damage and long-term complications. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the potential benefits and risks of using corticosteroids as an adjunctive treatment in children diagnosed with septic arthritis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), LILACS, the WHO trials portal, ClinicalTrials.gov, and Google Scholar. The search included studies published up to April 17, 2018, without language restrictions. The analysis included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children aged two months to 18 years who were diagnosed with septic arthritis and received corticosteroids in addition to antibiotics or other therapies such as surgical drainage, intra-articular puncture, arthroscopic irrigation, or debridement. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. Key outcomes considered were pain levels, ability to perform daily activities, normal joint function, duration of antibiotic treatment, length of hospital stay, and the occurrence of adverse events. The evidence was assessed using the GRADE methodology, and a summary of findings was created. Two RCTs, involving a total of 149 children aged three months to 18 years, were included in the analysis. The most commonly affected joints were the hips and knees. These studies were conducted in Costa Rica and Israel. In both trials, dexamethasone was administered intravenously at doses ranging from 0.15 to 0.2 mg/kg every six to eight hours for four days. The comparator in both studies was a placebo. Patients with any degree of immunodeficiency or immunosuppression were excluded. The longest follow-up period was one year. Neither study reported data on daily activities or hospital length of stay. Both studies employed appropriate methods for randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding, and were judged to have a low risk of selection and performance bias. However, both trials had significant losses to follow-up, leading to a high risk of attrition bias and selective outcome reporting. As a result, the quality of evidence for all outcomes was graded as low due to concerns about study limitations and imprecision. At 12 months of follow-up, corticosteroids were associated with a higher likelihood of pain resolution, with a risk ratio (RR) of 1.33 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03 to 1.72; P = 0.03). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 13 (95% CI 6 to 139), with an absolute risk difference of 24% (95% CI 5% to 43%). Similarly, corticosteroids were associated with improved normal joint function at 12 months, with an RR of 1.32 (95% CI 1.12 to 1.57; P = 0.001). The NNTB was 13 (95% CI 7 to 33), with an absolute risk difference of 24% (95% CI 11% to 37%). Corticosteroids also reduced the duration of intravenous antibiotic treatment, with a mean difference (MD) of -2.77 days (95% CI -4.16 to -1.39). However, the length of hospital stay was not reported in either trial. One study involving 49 participants noted that dexamethasone treatment was associated with a shorter duration of intravenous antibiotic use and hospital stay, but specific data on hospital length of stay were not provided. In one trial involving 49 participants, 29 children were followed for 12 months, and no adverse effects of corticosteroid treatment were reported by parents. However, the quality of evidence was downgraded due to concerns about study limitations (high risk of attrition bias and selective reporting) and imprecision. In conclusion, the evidence supporting the use of corticosteroids as adjunctive therapy in children with septic arthritis is of low quality and is based on findings from two small trials involving 149 participants. Corticosteroids may increase the proportion of children who are pain-free and have normal joint function at 12 months, and they may reduce the duration of antibiotic treatment. However, the current evidence is insufficient to draw strong conclusions. Further randomized clinical trials with relevant outcomes are needed to better understand the role of corticosteroids in this context.
